what_it_does: Earth-observation satellites continuously photograph the planet, but the radio link from orbit to ground (the downlink) is so narrow that more than 90% of captured images never make it down. Standard on-board compression treats each image as independent, missing the fact that most of the Earth's surface changes very slowly — the same fields, roads, and coastlines appear in image after image from many satellites flying similar orbits. Earth+ uses other satellites in the constellation as a source of recent reference images: the ground station uploads a matching reference image to the satellite via the uplink, and the satellite's on-board processor compares its freshly captured image against the reference, transmitting only the pixels that changed (a technique called delta encoding). Because changes between closely-timed images of the same region are small, the delta is tiny, dramatically increasing effective downlink capacity without expensive hardware modifications.
